transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, they made me come here. The lieutenant did. I didn't even want to leave my shift, but I didn't really have a choice because of what happened down at the station. See, we were in the apparatus bay, and I was looking at the airway bags, and I just... I realized they weren't right. They were all wrong. So I started moving them. I had to move them into this specific pattern, a very precise arrangement that I just knew was the only right way for them to sit. 

And while I was doing it, I had to say the dispatch numbers out loud. I was just repeating the dispatch numbers over and over, matching them to the bags, because the numbers and the pattern, they go together, you have to do both at the same time. But then my lieutenant came over and he told me to stop. He told me to step away from the gear. But I couldn't do that. I wouldn't step away because... well, if I broke the sequence, if I didn't finish moving those bags while saying the numbers, the whole bay would go bad. The entire station would just go completely bad. It felt so heavy, like this massive pressure, and I knew I had to finish the sequence to keep everything from going bad. But he didn't understand, he just saw me moving the bags and wouldn't let me finish, and he pulled me off the floor, and now... well, now they sent me here to you because of it.
What did you mean by 'the whole bay would go bad' if you didn't finish the sequence?

Well, you know, it's hard to explain to someone who wasn't standing right there in the bay, but... when I say "go bad," I mean it literally. Like, the very air in the apparatus bay was getting thick, you know? It was getting heavy, like right before a massive thunderstorm rolls in and the pressure just drops and your ears pop. I could feel it pressing on my skin. And the airway bags—the blue ones, the red ones for pediatrics, all of them—they were sitting there on the shelves, and they were just... they were completely out of alignment with the dispatch numbers I was hearing in my head. 

If I didn't move them—if I didn't take the adult bag and put it exactly two inches to the left of the oxygen tank while saying "Dispatch 4-1-9," and then move the pediatric bag exactly parallel to it while saying "Dispatch 4-2-0"—the pressure was just going to keep building. The whole station would go bad. The rigs wouldn't start, or the oxygen lines would get contaminated, or... or something terrible would happen on our next call. I just knew it. It was this absolute certainty in my gut. It's like... like if you see a frayed wire next to a puddle of water. You just know you have to move it or someone's going to get electrocuted. 

But my lieutenant, he just didn't see the danger. He just saw me rearranging the bags and talking to myself. He didn't understand the sequence. He kept saying, "Step away from the gear, step away from the gear," but how could I? If I stopped halfway through, the sequence would be broken, and the badness—that heavy, terrible pressure—would just explode everywhere. That's why I wouldn't stop. That's exactly why they sent me here, because I was just trying to fix it, I was trying to save the bay, and he just pulled me away before I could finish the pattern. And now... now I don't even know what's happening back there because the pattern was never finished.
Did you think that not completing the sequence would actually cause the bad things you mentioned to happen, like the rigs not starting or the oxygen lines getting contaminated?

Well, I... I don't know exactly. I mean, I can't say for a hundred percent certain that it was going to be the rigs, or exactly how it would happen. It's not like I had a... a vision of the future or a maintenance manual in my head that said, you know, "If you don't move the blue airway bag exactly two inches, the alternator on Rig 42 is going to seize up," or "the brass fittings on the main O2 tanks are going to sheer off." I don't have a crystal ball. 

I was just... when I said that before, about the rigs or the oxygen, I was just trying to give you examples of what that kind of pressure feels like it could do. Because I don't actually know what the badness would manifest as. I just know it was there. It's like... okay, if you're on a scene, right? You walk into a house and you just get this immediate gut feeling that a patient is about to crash. You don't necessarily know if they're going to throw a fatal arrhythmia or if their airway is just going to completely close up on you, you just know that the bottom is about to drop out and you have to act right that second. 

That's exactly what the apparatus bay felt like. The physical bags and the dispatch numbers... if they aren't synced up perfectly, the energy just stagnates and gets completely toxic. The pressure just builds and builds and builds. So, did I think those specific things would happen? I don't know. I really don't. It could have been the rigs, it could have been the oxygen lines getting contaminated, it could have been our cardiac monitor throwing a random fault code right when we need to shock somebody. I don't know what breaks when that kind of pressure finally pops. I just know something breaks. 

And that's the most frustrating part about all of this, because my lieutenant—and look, he's a good guy, he's been on the job for twenty years, he knows his protocols—but he just doesn't feel the shift in the air. He just looks at the morning checklist. But the checklist doesn't mean a damn thing if the sequence is broken. If the sequence is broken, the whole foundation of the station is rotten. So I can't sit here and give you a specific answer on what exactly was going to fail, I just know that the pressure was screaming at me that something was going to give, and I was the only one trying to stop it. And now I'm here, and I have no idea what's happening back at the station because I never got to finish.
Do you think that other people would understand the importance of moving the airway bags in the specific pattern you described if they were in your position?

Would other people understand? No. No, I really don't think they would, and I mean... they didn't, right? That's... that's the whole reason I'm sitting in this chair in your office right now. Like I was saying earlier, they sent me here specifically because at the station I kept moving the airway bags into that pattern, the one I just absolutely knew was right, and I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud to sync it all up. And when my lieutenant told me to stop, I wouldn't step away. I flat out refused a direct order because it felt like the whole bay would go bad if I broke the sequence. 

But to answer your question about if someone else was in my position... you have to understand the mindset of the guys I work with. You have to know how an EMT or a paramedic thinks. We are trained to look at tangible things, right? We look at massive hemorrhages, at compound fractures, at a twelve-lead EKG to see if there's ST elevation. We look at things you can touch, things you can measure with a blood pressure cuff or an oxygen gauge. So if my partner, or if the battalion chief walked in and stood exactly where I was standing in the apparatus bay... they wouldn't feel the pressure dropping. They wouldn't hear the numbers matching up with the colors of the bags. They just wouldn't get it at all. 

They don't have the... the receiver for it, I guess you could say. They're tuned to a completely different frequency. So when they looked at me, they didn't see a guy who was holding the whole structural integrity of the station together just by keeping that sequence going. They just saw a thirty-eight-year-old man in his station boots, standing by the rigs, refusing to step away from the gear when his commanding officer told him to. 

It’s incredibly isolating, honestly. It really is. Because you’re standing there doing the most important job in the world right in that exact second, literally keeping the badness from crushing everyone, and everyone else just thinks you're being insubordinate or messing with the inventory. They just think you're crazy. So no, they wouldn't understand the importance of it. If they understood, they would have helped me finish moving the bags instead of dragging me out of there and sending me to a psychiatrist.
Do you still believe that not completing the sequence of moving the airway bags and saying the dispatch numbers would have caused something bad to happen at the station?

I mean... like I was just saying a minute ago, yes. Absolutely I still believe it. Sitting in this office doesn't magically change what was happening back there. It doesn't change the pressure. I know I keep bringing this up, but you really have to understand that this is the entire reason they sent me here in the first place. 

They sent me here because I was standing there at the station, moving those airway bags into the pattern I knew was right, repeating the dispatch numbers out loud to lock the energy in, and when my lieutenant ordered me to step away from the gear, I wouldn't do it. I couldn't. I refused a direct order from a commanding officer I respect, and I didn't do that just to be a problem. I did it because I knew—and I still know, right this very second—that if I stepped away and broke the sequence, the whole bay would go bad. It’s not just a belief, it’s a physical reality. It’s like gravity. You don't stop believing in gravity just because you walk into a different room.

And honestly, sitting here right now, answering these questions, it's tearing me apart inside because my brain is just spinning about what happened after they dragged me out of there. Did someone just shove the blue and red bags back onto the shelf? Did they just toss them into the rig without finishing the numbers? Because if they did, that heavy, toxic energy is just pooling up in the corners of the station right now. It's like... it's like leaving a tourniquet on a patient's limb for way too long, you know? Eventually, the tissue just goes necrotic and dies. 

That's what's happening to the station. If the sequence wasn't finished, the badness is just seeping into the rigs, into the gear, into the oxygen lines, and I can't do a damn thing about it from this chair. I'm stuck here talking to you while the whole foundation of my station is probably rotting out from the inside. So yes, to answer your question, yes, I still believe it. I didn't risk my entire career, refuse a direct order, and get myself hauled off to a psychiatrist just for the fun of it. I did it because it was real, and it's still real, and finishing that pattern was the only thing keeping the badness at bay.
Do you think that the pressure and the badness you felt would still be present if someone else had completed the sequence of moving the airway bags and saying the dispatch numbers?

I mean... theoretically? I guess? But you're kind of missing the practical reality of the situation. Like... okay, I know I keep repeating myself, I know I probably sound like a broken record about why they sent me here to see you in the first place, but I keep bringing it up because it's the entire core of the problem! I was moving those airway bags into that specific pattern because I knew it was the only right way to do it, and I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud to keep the sync going. And when my lieutenant told me to stop, I absolutely refused to step away. I couldn't. I keep telling you that because if I broke the sequence, the whole bay was going to go bad. The toxicity would just spill everywhere. 

So, could someone else have finished it and stopped the pressure? The thing is... no one else knew the sequence. If my partner or the lieutenant had just stepped in and started grabbing the bags, they would have completely messed it up. They wouldn't know which dispatch number pairs with the blue bag versus the red bag. It’s like... it’s like if you’re doing CPR on a code, right? You can't just have some random bystander step in and do compressions at forty beats a minute and expect the patient to survive. It has to be exactly one hundred to one hundred and twenty beats a minute. The rhythm has to be perfect. You have to push hard and fast. 

If someone else had stepped into my spot in the apparatus bay, they wouldn't have felt the pressure building. They wouldn't have heard the numbers matching the colors. They would have just tossed the gear back on the shelf and completely shattered the pattern. They'd cross the wires, so to speak, and probably make the badness happen even faster. 

So, sure, if there was some hypothetical other EMT who had the exact same... the same receiver in his head that I do, and he stepped in on the exact right beat and said the exact right dispatch number while moving the bag two inches to the left... maybe. Maybe the pressure would have lifted and the badness would have cleared out. But that’s not what happened. I was the only one who could feel it, which is exactly why I couldn't obey the lieutenant's order to step away. I had to be the one to finish it, and they didn't let me. And now the sequence is just hanging there, unfinished.
Do you think there's any possibility that you might be wrong about the importance of moving the airway bags in that specific pattern?

Am I wrong? Is there a possibility...? Look, doc, I... I know I keep coming back to this. I know I've basically told you this exact same thing over and over since I walked through your door, but you keep asking me these questions that circle right back to it, and you have to understand that this is the absolute crux of the whole situation. 

They sent me here—literally forced me off shift and made me come see you—specifically because at the station, I kept moving those airway bags into a pattern that I *knew* was right. Not a pattern I guessed was right, or hoped was right. I knew it. I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud to keep the whole thing anchored, and when my lieutenant told me to stop, I wouldn't step away. I just couldn't do it. I refused. 

Now, I want you to really think about that for a second. I've got years on the job. I have my associate's degree, I have a career, I have a commanding officer who I respect immensely. Do you really think I would look my lieutenant in the eye and refuse a direct order if there was even a fraction of a percent of a chance that I was wrong? You don't just throw all your training and your career out the window on a whim. I wouldn't step away because it felt like the whole bay would go bad if I broke the sequence. It wasn't a hypothesis. It was an absolute, undeniable reality happening right in front of me. 

If you're out in the field and you see a patient with an arterial bleed, do you stop and think, 'Gee, is there a possibility I'm wrong about needing to apply a tourniquet?' No! You see the bright red blood spurting, you feel the urgency, and you act. You do what has to be done to save them. That’s exactly what this was. When you're standing right in the middle of it, when you feel the heavy toxicity pressing down on the room and you know that finishing the pattern and saying the numbers is the only thing holding it back... you don't second-guess it. You just do your job to keep everyone safe. So, no. There is absolutely no possibility I was wrong. None at all.
Is there anything that could happen or anything someone could tell you that would make you change your mind about the importance of moving the airway bags in that specific pattern?

Look, doc, I feel like we're just going in circles here. You keep trying to find some kind of crack in my story, like if you just phrase the question differently, I'll suddenly snap my fingers and say, oh wow, you're right, I made it all up. But I can't do that. I know I keep beating this same drum, and I know I've told you the exact same thing about why they pulled me off shift and stuck me in this room, but I have to keep saying it because it's the truth. 

Could someone tell me something to change my mind? No. Could something happen to make me see it differently? No. Because... look, just put yourself in my boots for one second. Think about the sheer magnitude of what happened. I've explained how I was physically placing those airway bags into that exact, necessary configuration, right? I was vocalizing the dispatch codes, saying them out loud to keep the whole system anchored. And then my lieutenant—a guy I have worked under for years, a guy I respect more than almost anyone else in the department—is standing right there barking at me to drop the gear and step back. 

And I defied him. I flat-out refused to back down when he ordered me to stop. 

Do you think a simple conversation, or someone showing me a textbook, is going to make me go, oh, sure, I guess I just threw my entire career and my reputation away for absolutely nothing? No! Because in that moment, the threat wasn't just some abstract idea. It wasn't a mistake. If I had stopped, if I had let that sequence fracture before it was completed, the entire apparatus bay was going to turn completely toxic. The whole place would have just gone completely bad. I could literally feel the pressure of it in my teeth, in my chest, like the air was turning to lead. 

When you experience something that real, when you are standing between your crew and a complete catastrophe... you don't just change your mind later because someone in a nice office asks you to. It happened. I had to do it. So, no, there are no magic words you or my lieutenant or anyone else can say that will make me un-feel that reality.
Is it possible for you to consider the idea that the sequence of moving the airway bags and saying the dispatch numbers might not be as crucial as you believe it is?

I just... I don't understand why we keep hammering at this exact same spot, doc. It’s like you’re just waiting for me to give up and say what you want to hear, like you're trying to wear me down. But I can't do that. Is it possible for me to consider it wasn't crucial? No. Absolutely not. 

And I know I keep saying this, I know I've basically given you the exact same rundown multiple times now, but you have to understand the reality of the situation. They sent me here—they forced me into this office—because at the station, I kept moving those airway bags into a pattern that I knew was right. I wasn't guessing, I wasn't playing a game. I knew it was right. I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud, over and over, locking the whole thing in, keeping it stabilized. And I wouldn't step away when my lieutenant told me to stop. I defied a direct order from a superior officer. I wouldn't step away because it felt like the whole bay would go completely bad if I broke the sequence. 

The toxicity was right there, pressing down on us, getting heavier by the second. You're asking me if I can just... what, pretend that feeling wasn't real? Pretend that the pattern didn't matter? It was the only thing keeping the air breathable, keeping the whole system from collapsing in on itself. When you're the only one who can see the structural integrity of the room failing, you don't just walk away because someone tells you to. You hold the line. So no, I can't consider that it wasn't crucial. It was the single most crucial thing happening in that station, and if I hadn't done it, we wouldn't even be having this conversation right now because everything would have just gone completely bad.
Do you think the pressure and badness you felt would still exist if nobody else was around to witness it?

Would it still exist if... Doc, listen to me. Listen to what I am actually saying. It has absolutely nothing to do with whether anyone was watching me. It’s not a performance. The pressure, that... that heavy, toxic weight... it doesn't just magically appear because people are standing around. I mean, I don't know how many different ways I can explain the exact same event to you. We keep going over this, and I keep telling you why they sent me here in the first place, but you seem to think this is all dependent on an audience. 

I'm going to say it again, because it's the only thing that matters here. They sent me here—they literally forced me off shift and into this evaluation—because at the station, I kept moving the airway bags into a specific pattern. A pattern I knew was right. I was physically moving them, aligning them, and repeating the dispatch numbers out loud, over and over, because that was the anchor. That was the only thing stabilizing the room. 

It didn't matter that my lieutenant walked in. His presence didn't create the badness, and him leaving wouldn't have fixed it. When he told me to stop, I wouldn't step away. I couldn't. I defied a direct order from my lieutenant because it felt like the whole bay would go completely bad if I broke the sequence. If I had been entirely alone in the station, on a Sunday at three in the morning with not a single soul around, the air would have still turned to lead. The toxicity would have still been pressing down on my chest. The structural integrity of the room was failing, doc. I still would have had to arrange those bags and say those numbers to keep the bay from going bad. 

The reality of the situation exists whether there are witnesses or not. You have to understand that. The threat was real, the sequence was necessary, and the fact that they pulled me off shift for doing what had to be done to protect the station just... it blows my mind that we are still trying to find a way to make this sound like it wasn't actually happening.
Do you think the airway bags would still be in the wrong position if you weren't thinking about them?

Doc... I really, truly don't get what you're trying to prove with these thought experiments. "If I wasn't thinking about them." The airway bags are physical objects, okay? They're heavy, they're made of reinforced canvas, they have actual mass and take up space in the real world. My thoughts don't magically move them around. They were in the wrong position because they were physically placed wrong by whoever touched them last, not because I was just sitting in a chair daydreaming about it. 

I mean... I know I sound like a broken record here. I know I keep bringing us right back to the exact same incident, but you keep asking questions that completely ignore the reality of what actually happened! Listen to the facts of why they sent me here. They sent me to this forced evaluation because I wasn't just *thinking* about things. I was acting on them. I was physically at the station, taking those airway bags and moving them into the pattern that I knew was right. It was a tangible, physical action. I was dragging them across the floor. And the dispatch numbers... I wasn't just thinking those either. I was repeating them out loud, over and over, verbalizing them into the room so the sound would anchor the space. 

That's why my lieutenant got involved in the first place. He didn't read my mind, he saw me doing the work, and he told me to stop. And I wouldn't. I completely refused to step away from those bags when he gave me a direct order. Because... well, like I've been telling you this whole time, if I broke that sequence, if I didn't finish physically arranging them and saying the numbers, it felt like the entire bay was going to go completely bad. The physical space was going to become completely toxic. 

So, no, my thoughts don't dictate where the bags are. The bags were in the wrong spot, and I had to physically fix them, and that's the reality of why I'm sitting in this office right now. Whether I think about them or not doesn't change the physical danger we were all in.
Do you think that your actions of moving the airway bags and saying the dispatch numbers actually had any effect on the physical world?

Are you... are you even listening to the words coming out of my mouth, doc? I feel like I'm talking to a brick wall here. I literally just explained how physical this was, and you're asking me if it had an effect on the physical world? Yes! Yes, absolutely it did! That is the entire point of everything I have been trying to tell you for this entire session! 

I'm not talking about some spiritual, metaphorical, in-my-head kind of effect. I am talking about actual, tangible, physical reality. The molecules in the air. The atmospheric pressure in the room. I mean, I know I'm repeating myself, I know we keep circling this exact same drain, but I have to make you understand why they forced me into this evaluation. When I was at the station, dragging those heavy canvas airway bags across the concrete floor, I wasn't just doing it for my health. I kept moving them into that specific pattern because I knew, without a shadow of a doubt, that it was the right configuration to physically stabilize the space. 

And the dispatch numbers... when I was repeating them out loud, over and over, it wasn't just breath. The sound waves, the actual vibration of my voice hitting the walls and the rigs, it was physically anchoring the room. It was a mechanical countermeasure holding back the toxicity that was building up in the air. 

So when you ask if it had an effect on the physical world, look at the result! The bay didn't collapse. The air didn't turn to poison. Because I held the line. That's exactly why I wouldn't step away when my lieutenant came out and told me to stop. He gave me a direct order to knock it off and step away from the equipment, and I flat-out refused. I defied a superior officer because I knew the physical consequences of stopping. If I had broken that sequence—if I had stopped aligning those bags and speaking those numbers—the physical reality is that the whole bay would have gone completely bad. The air would have become unbreathable. The pressure would have literally crushed the structural integrity of the room. 

So yes, doc. It had an effect. The most important effect possible. It kept the physical world intact right there in the station. It's basic cause and effect. Action and reaction. I did the physical work, and the bay didn't go bad. I don't know how I can make that any clearer for you.
Do you think your belief in the importance of the airway bag sequence is related to any thoughts or feelings you've been having outside of work?

Outside of work? Doc, listen, outside of work, it's a completely different universe. You're asking if I have these intense thoughts or feelings at home tying into the sequence, but the truth is, when I'm not on shift... I don't have much of anything going on. At all. There is no grand connection because there is just... nothing. 

Most days, I go back to my apartment and I just sit. Literally, I will just sit in the exact same spot in my living room for hours. It’s just... empty. There’s trash, literally just piles of trash sitting right there in the corner of the room, and I stare at it, and I know it needs to go out to the dumpster, but it just stays there. And my fridge... man, I’ve got food still sitting in the fridge from God knows when. I used to be the guy who cooked, right? I used to actually make dinners, prep things, but now? The food just sits in there going bad because I can't even bring myself to open the door and do anything with it. 

I used to have a life outside the station. I used to call the guys up, we'd get a pickup game of basketball going, run the court, sweat it out and hang out. I haven't called them in I don't even know how long. I don't call them for basketball, I don't cook like I used to, I don't take out the trash... because I just can't get myself to care. I can't get myself to start anything. It's like the starter motor in my chest is just completely ripped out. The part of me that tells me to care about my own life is just completely shut off. 

So if you're trying to draw a line between me physically protecting the bay at work and what I feel at home... they aren't the same. At work, I had to act to stop the badness. At home, I can't even muster the energy to care if the food is rotting right in front of me. I just sit there. I can't start a single thing.
Do you think other people would benefit from knowing and following the same sequence of moving the airway bags and saying the dispatch numbers?

Would they benefit? I... I don't know if they could even handle it, doc. I really don't. I mean, look at how they reacted when I actually did it. Look at the exact reason they forced me into this room with you. 

I know I keep hammering on this, I know I've told you this same story like three times already today, but you have to look at the facts of why they sent me here in the first place. They sent me here because I was out there on the concrete, physically moving those heavy airway bags into the specific pattern I knew was right, and I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud to anchor the room. And when my lieutenant came out—when he marched right up to me and gave me a direct order to step away from the equipment—I wouldn't do it. I flat-out refused to stop. I stood my ground because I knew, I could literally feel it in the air, that if I broke that sequence, the whole bay was going to go completely bad. 

So if you're asking me if the other guys on the shift should be doing it? Sure, in a perfect world, yeah, it would be great if everyone knew how to stabilize the space. It would take the burden off me. But they don't get it. They don't see the mechanics of it. To them, it just looks like insubordination. They just see a guy defying his lieutenant. If I tried to teach them the sequence, they’d probably just mess it up. They wouldn't put the bags in the exact right spot, or they’d stumble on the dispatch numbers, or they'd just stop halfway through because they got bored or someone called their name. 

And that's the thing, doc—you can't just stop halfway. If someone else tried to do it and they broke the sequence, it would be catastrophic. The toxicity would just flood right in. The pressure would collapse everything. So, honestly? Maybe it’s better that they don't know. Maybe it's better that I was the one who took the fall for it, even if it means I'm sitting here being evaluated like I'm crazy. Because at least I had the discipline to see it through. I knew what had to be done to keep that bay from going bad, and I did it, no matter who was yelling at me to step away.
Do you think your belief in the sequence would change if someone else completed it and nothing bad happened?

I... well, look. You're asking a hypothetical question about something that isn't hypothetical to me. It's not just a thought experiment, doc. It's real. You keep trying to poke holes in this, asking "what if this" and "what if that," but you're ignoring the actual reality of what happened. 

I've told you this, I know I've told you this, but I really need you to understand the exact mechanics of why I am sitting in this chair right now. They didn't send me here because I had a weird thought. They sent me here because of what I physically did at the station. I was out there, on the floor, and I kept moving those heavy canvas airway bags into that very specific pattern. The pattern that I knew, with absolute certainty, was the right one. And I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud, over and over, letting the sound waves hit the walls to anchor the space. 

And then my lieutenant comes out, right? He marches up and tells me to stop. He gives me a direct, undeniable order to step away from the equipment. And I wouldn't do it. I refused. I stood there and I kept the sequence going because I could feel it—I could literally feel the pressure building, the toxicity right at the edge of the room. If I had listened to him, if I had broken that sequence and just walked away like a good little soldier, it felt like the whole bay would just go completely bad. The air, the structure, everything. 

So when you ask me if my belief would change if someone else did it... how could they? How could someone else possibly replicate the exact pressure, the exact tone of voice, the exact spatial alignment of those bags? They couldn't. They'd mess it up. And if they messed it up, the bay would go bad, and then everyone would see that I was right all along. But I wasn't going to let that happen. That's why I wouldn't step away. That's why I'm here. Because I actually did the work to keep it from going bad, and nobody else could have done it exactly the way it needed to be done.
Do you think your belief in the sequence would change if someone else completed it and nothing bad happened, and you were to witness it yourself?

Witness it myself? Doc, you're... you're really stuck on this "what if" train, aren't you? If I stood there and watched someone else do it... I just, I don't think you're grasping the absolute gravity of the situation that day. I know I sound like a broken record, I know I keep circling back to this same exact moment, but I have to make you understand the literal, physical reality of why they dragged me into this facility in the first place. 

It wasn't because I was sitting around passively watching other people do things. They sent me here because at the station, I was the one down on the concrete. I kept moving the airway bags—those bulky, heavy bags—into a pattern I knew was right. I was the one repeating the dispatch numbers out loud, making sure the acoustics hit the walls just right to anchor everything. 

So if I were just watching someone else? I wouldn't be able to just stand there and be a witness. Because think about what actually happened—when my lieutenant came out, when he was standing right over me, barking at me to stop... I wouldn't step away. He told me to stop, he gave me a direct, undeniable order, and I flat-out refused to step away because it felt like the whole bay would go bad if I broke the sequence. The air was getting so thick, doc, the pressure was immense. 

If I was just a bystander watching someone else try to do it, they would have messed up the pattern, they would have stumbled on the numbers, and the bay would have gone bad anyway. I couldn't just witness it. I had to be the one doing it. That's why I didn't stop when the lieutenant ordered me to, and that's exactly why they sent me here.
